status.detail: 587 photos from 28 visits (Apr 22 to Oct 6). Videos deleted.
YOLO11x-seg reference (2 s per photo). Benchmarked 28 faster settings: YOLO11s-seg@640 on OpenVINO runs at 55 ms per photo, YOLO11m-seg@1024 OpenVINO int8 at 185 ms keeps 85% of the cats.
Labels v5: 34 cats, 483 crops after three review rounds (links, names, splits) and the Jul 7 cutoff.
Local: DINOv2, CLIP, MegaDescriptor-T, SigLIP2, DINOv3 (B sizes). Helper sessions: DINOv2-L, DINOv3-L, SigLIP2-so400m, CLIP-L, MegaDescriptor-L, MiewID.
Done on DINOv2-B: duplicate removal, collar colour, burst pooling, whitening, re-ranking, learned heads (negative). Next: background masking ablation, coat-colour gating, recency prior.
pipeline.py v2 on OpenVINO: 0.28 s per photo end to end.

findings.title: Overnight: a vision model re-ranking the top 3 is the biggest jump so far
findings.body: Blind test, 40 queries from visits 6 onward, each one crop of a cat seen before. The embedding (DINOv2-B + recipe + query expansion) proposes its top 3 cats in shuffled order with 4 crops each, and I (Claude, vision) picked one or said 'none of these' without seeing the answers. Embedding alone: 23/40 right (57%). With Claude picking: 29/40 (72%). When the right cat was among the three, the pick was right 29 of 34 times (85%). 'None of these' was said 7 times and was correct 5 times, so it doubles as a new-cat detector. All 8 cases where the pick beat the embedding were look-alike pairs the embedding confuses: Rocky vs Onyx (both black with blue collars, the vision model used fur length and white chest hairs), Sylph vs Casper vs Mister Buttons (white kittens, it used the grey head smudge), Shovel vs Griffin vs Papaya (orange, it used the white blaze and collar). Two misses: it called Paprika 'none' and confused Casper with Sylph. Cost: one vision call per new cluster per visit. That is cheap at this scale, and the review page already has an 'Ask Claude' button wired the same way.

findings.title: Scored per group, a visit's photos of a known cat are named right 74% first, 93% in the top 3
findings.body: What you would confirm in practice is one group per cat per visit, not single photos. Scoring 58 (visit, cat) groups of cats seen before, with DINOv2-B + recipe + query expansion: if each photo in the group takes its single best match in that cat's history and the group averages those, the right cat is first 74% of the time and in the top 3 93%. Averaging each photo's top 3 matches is worse (67%), and using only the cat's last two visits is worse too (67%): one good old photo from the right angle beats several recent ones.

findings.title: Face crops: as good as the whole body, +2 points when combined
findings.body: OWLv2 (open-vocabulary detection, prompt 'a cat's face') found a head box in about three quarters of crops. Faces were re-cut from the full-resolution originals and embedded with DINOv2. The face alone matches cats across visits about as well as the whole body (top-1 0.54 vs 0.54 for B, set-level top-1 0.63 vs 0.60). Averaging face and body similarity gives +2 points top-1 (0.56) and the best open-set accuracy so far (0.62). Black and tuxedo cats gain only 1 to 3 points (0.42 to 0.44 with DINOv2-S), so faces do not solve the black-cat problem. OWLv2 costs about 3 s per crop on CPU, too slow for the fast pipeline. A small dedicated cat-face detector would be needed to use this.

findings.title: Detector: a 37x faster YOLO keeps 77 to 85% of the cats
findings.body: A helper benchmarked 28 detector settings against the YOLO11x-seg reference (975 cats, 1,965 ms per photo on 4 CPU cores). OpenVINO runs the same models 2.2 to 3.4 times faster than PyTorch with the same accuracy, while ONNX Runtime is slower than PyTorch. Fast setting: YOLO11s-seg at 640px on OpenVINO, 53 to 57 ms per photo, keeping 77% of the reference's cats at 94% agreement. 640px loses small cats in group shots. Balanced setting: YOLO11m-seg at 1024px on OpenVINO int8, conf 0.25, 185 ms per photo, keeping 85% of the cats and 94% of the confident ones. YOLO26 is no better than YOLO11, and box-only models are only 10 to 20% faster than segmentation ones.

findings.title: Overnight: graph tricks with no labels add 3 to 5 points
findings.body: Three label-free transductive tricks, tested in an honest online replay where each visit only sees photos from itself and earlier visits (DINOv2-B + recipe). Baseline: known-cat top-1 0.56, top-3 0.85. Alpha query expansion (each crop averaged with its 5 nearest neighbours, weighted by similarity cubed): 0.61 / 0.87. Graph diffusion on a mutual 20-nearest-neighbour graph: 0.60 / 0.90. Visit consolidation (cluster the visit, pool each crop with its predicted group): 0.59 / 0.89. Stacking them over-smooths and loses ground, so use one at a time. On the whole dataset at once, diffusion lifts retrieval mAP from 0.47 to 0.57. DINOv2-S gains less (+1 to 2 points).

findings.title: Shelter listings as a reference: dropped
findings.body: Matching the shelter's current adoption listings against your photos mostly paired old, since-adopted café cats with newer listed cats that merely look similar (Toast came after Scythe was adopted and looks different). A listing only shows who is available now, not who was at the café on a given day, so it is out of the pipeline for now.

findings.title: The big models barely help; animal re-ID models lose
findings.body: Labels v5, same recipe. Cross-visit top-1 / known-cat top-3: DINOv2-L 0.56 / 0.85, DINOv2-B 0.54 / 0.87, DINOv2-S 0.54 / 0.87, SigLIP2-so400m 0.46 / 0.78, MiewID 0.46 / 0.70, DINOv3-L 0.46 / 0.64, MegaDescriptor-L 0.41 / 0.70. Averaging DINOv2 L, B and S gives the best known-cat top-3 so far, 0.92. Input resolution (224, 336, 448) changes little. The models trained specifically for animal re-identification do worse here than generic self-supervised features.

findings.title: Round 3: splits, a mid-visit adoption, and the Jul 7 cutoff
findings.body: Your split letters relabeled 40 crops. Bean was really Gobi Bear and Sox; the white-cat groups were Sylph, Casper and Mister Buttons; CalicoKit was Callie and Casper. You named both calico kittens from Oct 6 Callie. Her collar is pink at 4:13 pm and yellow at 4:34 pm, so she was adopted during that visit. The collar rule now allows pink or blue to yellow within one visit too, never back. TuxYellow is Paddington Bear after adoption. Cats last seen on or before Jul 7 are cut (Jade, Martha, Shayla and three unnamed early kittens). Labels v5: 34 cats, 483 crops. Within-visit grouping F1 rose to 0.89. Known-cat top-3 fell to 0.84 to 0.88, because the white-kitten and tabby splits separate cats the model was treating as one. That is the honest number now.

findings.title: Your names merged 7 groups; one group was 3 cats
findings.body: You gave 39 names. Seven names appeared on two or three of my groups, so those are now one cat each: Jade, Papaya, Sox, Paprika, Scythe, Midnight, Dawn. CalicoKitYellow was three cats: a tabby-calico kitten with a pink collar, a calico kitten with a yellow 'Calli...' collar, and Yoplait (the adult in the basket). Labels v4: 46 cats, 525 crops. The merges add longer-gap matches (for example Papaya in April and July), so scores dip slightly. Averaging DINOv2-B and -S gives cross-visit top-1 0.57, and the right cat is in the top 3 for 95% of known-cat crops.

findings.title: Your review: 33 of my 73 uncertain links were right
findings.body: You confirmed 33 cross-visit links and rejected 40, so my guesses about which kitten grew into which cat were barely better than a coin flip. The rejected ones are dropped for now, as you suggested. Of the 30 'model disagrees with my label' pairs, 3 were the same cat. With your names, BlackBlue and SmokeKit are Onyx, and OrangeYellow is Shovel. Labels v3: 525 crops across 53 cats, 4 uncertain links left. On these cleaner labels, for a cat seen before, the right one is in the top 3 suggestions 94 to 96% of the time (87% on my labels), and top-1 is 0.53.

findings.title: Collar code: blue = male, pink = female, yellow = adopted
findings.body: Your rule became a compatibility score: same colour gets a bonus. Pink vs blue is impossible. Yellow after pink or blue is allowed (an adoption), and yellow before pink or blue is impossible, as are two colours in one visit. Checking my labels against it exposed collar-detector noise rather than label errors: red pants read as pink, a blue towel and jeans as blue, and neighbours' collars in cat piles. The detector now ignores other cats' pixels and rejects colours that also fill the surrounding background. Pink and red count as one family, and blue must be bright. Its agreement with each cat's usual colour went from 90% to 97%. Scoring-wise the code matches the simple same/different collar score, since few pink-to-yellow transitions are labeled, but it encodes an impossible match (pink vs blue) that pure similarity can't.

findings.title: Current best recipe
findings.body: DINOv2 on the plain crop, centered, burst shots pooled, plus the collar code and a zero-shot coat-pattern gate. On labels v3, single model: DINOv2-B top-1 0.54 and known-cat top-3 0.94; DINOv2-S top-1 0.53 and top-3 0.96 at a quarter of the cost. Averaging DINOv2-B and -S gives the best top-1 so far, 0.58. Adding MegaDescriptor-T gives the best end-to-end balance (0.69), with the right cat in the top 3 for 96% of known-cat crops.

findings.title: Patterned cats are easy, black cats and tabbies are hard
findings.body: Cross-visit top-1 by coat: calico/tortie 0.83, colourpoint/white 0.68, orange 0.49, tuxedo/bicolour 0.42, solid black 0.35, tabby 0.35. Calico patches work like a fingerprint. Black cats differ mainly in eye colour, size, fur length and collar, and generic embeddings barely see those. For black cats, collars (and the names written on them) carry most of the signal.

findings.title: Fast pipeline v2: 0.28 s per photo on 4 CPU cores
findings.body: catid/pipeline.py now runs YOLO11s-seg at 640px and DINOv2-S, both on OpenVINO. Matching uses query expansion over the visit and the roster, scores a group by each photo's best match, and calls a new cat at a calibrated 0.71 threshold. On the Oct 6 visit it takes 277 ms per photo end to end (detect 95, embed 89, decode 40, collar 38), even while another job was using the CPU, against 820 ms for v1 and about 2.5 s for the research setup. Replaying Oct 6 against earlier visits: known cats named right first 62%, in the top 3 81%, and new cats flagged 9 of 9.

findings.title: Two detections in one photo are usually the same cat
findings.body: Of 215 labeled same-photo detection pairs, 155 were the same cat: YOLO splits a cat at the collar or a hand, or fires twice (cat + dog class). The textbook rule 'detections in one photo are different individuals' would be wrong most of the time here. Merging detections whose masks overlap by more than 50% removes 148 duplicates (78% of them) and wrongly merges 8% of real pairs, mostly cats piled together. Within-visit grouping F1 jumped from 0.74 to 0.83.

findings.title: Masking out the background hurts
findings.body: Greying out everything outside the cat's segmentation mask was meant to stop the model matching laps and couches. On DINOv2-B it loses about 3 to 6 points of top-1 and known-cat top-3 versus the plain crop. The mask cuts off the collar and softens the silhouette, and DINOv2 already ignores most background. Plain crops are the default now.

findings.title: Scoring end-to-end, and why it is balanced
findings.body: The realistic test replays visits in date order: cluster each visit's crops, match each cluster to cats confirmed on earlier visits or call it new, then add the visit to the roster as if you confirmed it. About 45% of crops are a cat's first appearance, so plain accuracy rewards a model that says 'new' a lot (a weak model topped that table). The headline is now balanced: the average of 'known cat named right' and 'new cat called new'.

findings.title: Collar colour is the single best cheap feature
findings.body: Segmentation masks stop at the collar, so the colour is read from a 10px ring around the mask. Pink collars are pale (saturation 0.25 to 0.55) and blue jeans are everywhere, so each colour has its own rule. When it fires it is almost never wrong; it fires on roughly a third of crops. Adding it as a soft bonus or penalty lifts cross-visit top-1 from 0.41 to 0.46 on DINOv2-B.

findings.title: The model is a good label auditor
findings.body: Within one visit the model is reliable, so a crop whose closest same-visit neighbour has a different label is worth a second look. In the first 24 such pairs, 4 were my labeling mistakes (for example, the orange-and-white cat on the Aug 6 couch is the yellow-collar cat). Those are fixed in labels v2. The rest are queued for you in the Review tab.

findings.title: Café-specific priors that help: recency and coat pattern
findings.body: Cats get adopted and stop appearing, so a cat seen on a recent visit gets a small bonus (exp(-days/21) weighted 0.1). That lifts 'right cat among known cats' from 0.50 to 0.54. A zero-shot coat-pattern classifier (CLIP with prompts for tuxedo, calico, tortie, colorpoint and so on, after subtracting each prompt's average pull, which otherwise makes everything 'colorpoint') used as a soft gate adds about 1 point to DINOv2 and 3 to 4 points to weaker models.

findings.title: Some collars carry the cat's name
findings.body: Handwritten names are visible on several collars (Jade, Rocky, '... Bean'). They are anchors for cross-visit identity in the labels, and reading them with OCR is a candidate heuristic.

findings.title: DINOv2 beats CLIP and the animal re-ID model (so far)
findings.body: With the same recipe (centering, burst pooling, collar colour), DINOv2-B reaches cross-visit top-1 0.46 and set top-3 0.73. CLIP ViT-B/16 gets 0.29 and MegaDescriptor-T 0.28, even though MegaDescriptor was trained for animal re-identification. Averaging DINOv2 with them does not raise top-1, but nudges set top-3 and open-set accuracy up. Large models are still running in helper sessions.

findings.title: Training on my labels makes it worse
findings.body: A projection head trained with supervised contrastive loss, tested on held-out visits (5-fold leave-visits-out), loses 5 to 20 points of top-1 in every variant tried: linear, MLP, identity-initialised residual, cross-visit-only positives, shrinkage LDA. A zero-epoch head reproduces the raw score exactly, so this is overfitting, not a bug: about 50 cats with noisy cross-visit links are too few to learn identity that transfers to new visits. More confirmed cross-visit links from your review are the data this needs.

findings.title: Same visit is easy, a new visit is hard
findings.body: Grouping crops of one visit by cat reaches B-cubed F1 0.83. Recognising a cat on a different visit gives top-1 around 0.4, and the right cat is in the top 3 about 70% of the time at the set level. Kittens change fast (eye colour, size, colourpoint darkening), so the gallery has to keep updating.

findings.title: Newer is not better: DINOv3-B is worse than DINOv2-B here
findings.body: With the same recipe, DINOv3-B (CLS token, 320px) gets cross-visit top-1 0.37 against 0.50 for DINOv2-B, and averaging the two does not help. A helper session is testing whether pooling DINOv3's patch tokens changes this.

findings.title: The coat gate cannot be folded into DINOv2
findings.body: A linear probe on DINOv2 features trained to reproduce CLIP's coat call agrees with it only 56% of the time, and gating with it adds nothing. The coat gate helps because CLIP sees colour patterns differently, so it stays a separate (optional) model in the accurate setting.

findings.title: Keypoint matching (DISK + LightGlue) carries no identity signal
findings.body: The classic wildlife re-ID re-ranker matches local keypoints between a crop and its top-30 candidates. A helper ran it on 6,000 pairs. Among labeled candidate pairs, inlier counts separate same-cat from different-cat at AUC 0.49 to 0.52, which is chance. Fur on deforming cats in different poses doesn't give the stable keypoints that rigid stripe or spot patterns do, and the candidates already share coat colour. Not worth its 1+ s per pair.

findings.title: Patch pooling, including only the cat's own patches, loses to the CLS token
findings.body: A helper compared DINOv2-B's CLS token against mean and GeM pooling of patch tokens, and against pooling only the patches inside the cat mask. CLS on the plain crop is best (top-1 0.49 on the v1 labels). Mask-weighted pooling beats plain pooling (0.39 to 0.41 vs 0.27) but never beats CLS, and CLS plus mask-mean ties CLS.

findings.title: Building the roster with no labels at all: F1 0.67
findings.body: Clustering all 398 labeled-cat crops from all 28 visits at once, with no labels (DINOv2-B + recipe + query expansion, average linkage, same-photo cannot-link): B-cubed F1 0.67, ARI 0.60, 63 clusters for 35 real cats. Clusters are mostly pure (precision 0.75) but cats split across visits (recall 0.60). So the system could propose a roster from scratch that you mainly merge, rather than having to un-mix it.

findings.title: Forcing one cat per group within a visit doesn't help
findings.body: Making assignment within a visit one-to-one (Hungarian matching, so two groups cannot both claim the same known cat) slightly lowered set-level top-1 from 0.74 to 0.72. New cats' groups steal known cats' names under the constraint. A learned new-vs-known classifier over cluster features (score, margin, size, days since last seen, collar agreement) also did not beat a tuned threshold. The vision-model 'none of these' answer is the better new-cat signal.
